identity.title: Agnostic Active Learning Is Always Better Than Passive Learning

problem.claim: Characterize the optimal query complexity of agnostic active learning in the non-realizable case and determine whether it can always improve on passive learning.

gap.claim: Prior general analyses retained disagreement-related or similar complexity factors, yielding improvements only in restricted cases; universal benefits were previously unknown.

contributions.claim: Provides what the authors describe as the first sharp characterization of optimal first-order query complexity for agnostic active learning.
Proposes a general active-learning algorithm that achieves the characterized query complexity.
Removes additional complexity factors from the leading term, implying benefits for every concept class in the non-realizable setting.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish the work as the first sharp characterization and as making universal active-learning improvement possible, which they state was not previously known.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report that the optimal query complexity has a leading term always strictly smaller than passive supervised-learning sample complexity, by a factor proportional to the best-in-class error rate.
The authors report that their characterization removes the disagreement coefficient and related complexity factors from the leading term.

narrative_sequence.summary: Frames universal improvement of agnostic active learning over passive learning as a long-standing theoretical question.
Contrasts the result with earlier general analyses whose leading terms included disagreement-related factors and helped only in restricted cases.
Introduces a sharp optimal query-complexity characterization and an algorithm attaining it.
States that the leading term is always strictly smaller than passive sample complexity and that every concept class benefits in the non-realizable case.
Characterizes the work as settling the driving question of the preceding research program.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs a quantitative comparison with the structural change responsible for it: a leading-term improvement and removal of disagreement-related factors.

lessons.interpretation: This alignment makes a broad theoretical claim easier to assess conceptually by linking the headline advantage to a specific complexity-term distinction.
lessons.application: When presenting a theoretical improvement, state both the quantitative comparison and which term or assumption differs from prior general bounds.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the result has no meaningful baseline or term-level decomposition.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the formal hypotheses, query and sample-complexity definitions, algorithm details, or theorem statements.
The reported factor proportional to best-in-class error rate is not quantified more precisely, and no proof or experimental details are supplied.
The abstract does not identify the exact scope of concept classes or parameter regimes covered by the universal implication.
